fields.title: Tell Me the Story – Book 6: The Greatest Rescue
fields.subtitle: The Life of Jesus: His Last Week, His Death and His Rising Again
fields.description: Twenty-two Bible stories for children aged 6 to 10 that finish the Life of Jesus, each short enough to read aloud: the shining mountain, Palm Sunday, the Last Supper, the garden, the cross, the empty tomb, Mary in the garden, the road to Emmaus, Thomas, breakfast on the beach and the ascension. Told honestly and gently, with a prayer and three questions to talk about after every story. The sixth book of Tell Me the Story.
fields.about_html:
Tell Me the Story is an original Ochorus storybook Bible for children aged 6 to 10, in eight books and three parts: Old Testament Stories, The Life of Jesus, and New Testament Stories. God is the hero of every story, and the whole Bible is one story that leads to Jesus.

Book 6, “The Greatest Rescue”, is the last book of the Life of Jesus and the heart of the whole series. It tells twenty-two stories from the Gospels and Acts: the Transfiguration, Jesus’ last week in Jerusalem, His arrest, trial, death and burial, and His rising again, from the empty tomb to breakfast on the beach, the Great Commission and the ascension. Where the Gospels themselves say an Old Testament promise came true, as they do with the donkey, the dividing of His clothes and the cry from the cross, a line called “The promise kept” says so.

The cross is told plainly and without graphic detail, and the questions for the grown-up help a child talk it through. Each story takes about four minutes to read aloud, and under each are three questions to talk about together, with answers for the grown-up reading along. It reads well through Holy Week and Easter.

qa.question: Which stories are in Book 6 of Tell Me the Story?
qa.answer: Twenty-two stories: the shining mountain, Mary's perfume, Palm Sunday, the children singing in the temple, the widow's two coins, Jesus washing feet, the Last Supper, the garden of Gethsemane, the arrest, Peter's denials, Jesus and Pilate, the cross, "It is finished", the burial, the empty tomb, Mary in the garden, the road to Emmaus, Jesus appearing to the disciples, Thomas, breakfast on the beach, the Great Commission and the ascension.

qa.question: How is the crucifixion told for young children?
qa.answer: Plainly and gently. The story says that Jesus was whipped, crowned with thorns and nailed to a cross, without dwelling on the details. It focuses on what Jesus said and did: forgiving the soldiers, promising paradise to the thief, caring for His mother, and "It is finished." The grown-up notes suggest letting a child ask whatever they need to.

qa.question: Is it good for reading at Easter?
qa.answer: Yes. Its stories follow the days of Holy Week, from Palm Sunday and the Last Supper to Good Friday and the empty tomb on Easter Sunday, and then the appearances of the risen Jesus.

qa.question: What is "The promise kept"?
qa.answer: A short line under some stories, used only where the Gospels themselves say an Old Testament promise came true: Zechariah's King on a donkey (Matthew 21:5), Psalm 8's children's praise (Matthew 21:16), Psalm 22's divided clothes and cry (John 19:24; Matthew 27:46), the Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7), and the whole Scripture explained on the road to Emmaus (Luke 24:27).

qa.question: Do I need to read Books 4 and 5 first?
qa.answer: No. Each book stands on its own, and Book 6 begins with a short introduction. Children who have read the earlier books will recognise Peter, Mary and Martha, Nicodemus, and the Old Testament stories that the road to Emmaus brings together.

qa.question: Which Bible translation does it use?
qa.answer: Every verse quoted with its reference is word for word from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB), which is in the public domain.

fields.title: Introduction: The Most Important Story
fields.body_html:
“But these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name.” — John 20:31

In the last book, Jesus did wonderful things. He healed the sick and stilled the storm and fed the hungry. He told stories about lost sheep and lost sons, and about a God who runs to welcome people home. And at the end of the book, He called His friend Lazarus out of the tomb.

But not everyone was glad. The religious leaders were jealous and afraid of Jesus, and they began to plan how to get rid of Him.

This book tells the most important part of the whole story. Jesus goes to Jerusalem for the last time. He rides into the city on a donkey while the crowds cheer. He eats a last meal with His friends. And then He is arrested, and put on trial, and nailed to a cross, and He dies.

That sounds like the saddest ending there could be. But it isn’t the ending.

Do you remember the very first promise God made, in the garden, on the day everything went wrong? He promised that one day a child would be born who would crush the snake’s head, even though the snake would hurt Him. Do you remember the lamb God provided on the mountain, instead of Isaac? And the Passover lamb, whose blood kept God’s people safe?

All of those stories were pointing to this one. Jesus came to rescue us from sin and death. And the only way to do it was to give His own life.

But on the third day, something happened that changed everything for ever.

Some parts of this book are sad, and some parts are hard. But keep reading. The end of this book is the happiest news the world has ever heard.

Dear Jesus, thank you for loving us so much that you gave your life for us. As we read this story, help us to understand how much you love us, and to believe in you. Amen.

study_questions.question: Why were the religious leaders against Jesus?
study_questions.answer: They were jealous of Him and afraid that people would follow Him instead of them, especially after He raised Lazarus.

study_questions.question: What were some of the Old Testament stories that pointed to what Jesus would do?
study_questions.answer: The promise in the garden that a child would crush the snake, the lamb God provided instead of Isaac, and the Passover lamb whose blood kept God’s people safe.

study_questions.question: Why do you think this is called “the most important story”?
study_questions.answer: Because it tells how Jesus died and rose again to rescue us from sin and death, which is the heart of the whole Bible.

fields.title: The Shining Mountain
fields.body_html:
“This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to Him!” — Matthew 17:5

One day Jesus took three of His disciples, Peter and James and John, and led them up a high mountain, where they could be alone.

And there, right in front of them, Jesus was changed. His face shone like the sun, and His clothes became as white as light. The disciples were seeing Jesus’ glory, the glory He had always had as God’s Son, shining out of Him.

Then suddenly two other people appeared, talking with Jesus. They were Moses and Elijah! Moses, who had led God’s people out of Egypt and received God’s law. And Elijah, the great prophet who had seen fire fall from heaven. They had lived hundreds of years before, and now here they were, talking with Jesus.

Peter didn’t know what to say. But he said something anyway. “Lord, it’s good for us to be here!” he said. “If You want, I’ll put up three shelters: one for You, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.”

While Peter was still speaking, a bright cloud came down and covered them. And a voice came from the cloud: “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to Him!”

When the disciples heard this, they fell face down on the ground, terrified.

But Jesus came and touched them. “Get up,” He said. “Don’t be afraid.”

And when they looked up, they saw no one except Jesus.

As they were coming down the mountain, Jesus told them, “Don’t tell anyone what you have seen until the Son of Man has been raised from the dead.”

Peter wanted to make three shelters, as if Moses and Elijah and Jesus were all equally important. But God the Father made it clear: Jesus is the one. Moses gave God’s law, and Elijah was the greatest of the prophets. But Jesus is God’s own beloved Son. He is the one we must listen to.

Before and after this, Jesus told His disciples something they didn’t want to hear. He was going to Jerusalem. There He would suffer and be killed. And on the third day He would rise again.

The disciples didn’t understand. But on the mountain, they had seen a glimpse of who Jesus really was. They would need to remember it in the dark days ahead.

Read it in your Bible: Matthew 17:1–9

Dear Jesus, thank you for showing your glory to your disciples. You are God’s beloved Son. Help me to listen to you. Amen.

study_questions.question: What happened to Jesus on the mountain?
study_questions.answer: His face shone like the sun and His clothes became as white as light, and Moses and Elijah appeared and talked with Him.

study_questions.question: What did the voice from the cloud say?
study_questions.answer: “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to Him!”

study_questions.question: God said, “Listen to Him!” How can we listen to Jesus today?
study_questions.answer: By reading and hearing His words in the Bible, praying, and doing what He says.

fields.title: Mary’s Gift
fields.body_html:
“And the house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume.” — John 12:3

Six days before the Passover festival, Jesus came to Bethany, the village where His friends Lazarus, Martha and Mary lived. They gave a special dinner for Jesus. Martha served the food, and Lazarus, whom Jesus had raised from the dead, sat at the table with Him.

Then Mary came in, carrying a jar of perfume. It wasn’t just any perfume. It was made from a plant called nard, and it was very, very expensive. It was worth about a whole year’s wages!

Mary poured the perfume over Jesus’ feet. Then she wiped His feet with her hair.

And the whole house was filled with the beautiful smell of the perfume.

But one of Jesus’ disciples, Judas Iscariot, objected. Judas was the one who would later betray Jesus. “Why wasn’t this perfume sold, and the money given to the poor?” he said. “It was worth three hundred silver coins!”

Judas didn’t really care about the poor. The Bible tells us that he looked after the disciples’ money bag, and he used to steal from it.

“Leave her alone,” said Jesus. “She has kept this perfume for the day of My burial. You will always have poor people with you, but you won’t always have Me.”

Mary loved Jesus so much that she gave Him the most precious thing she had. She didn’t care what it cost. She didn’t care what people thought. She just wanted to show Jesus how much she loved Him.

And somehow, Mary seemed to understand something the other disciples hadn’t understood yet. Jesus was going to die. In those days, people put perfume on the body of someone who had died. Mary was getting Jesus ready, even before it happened.

Jesus said that what Mary did would be remembered wherever the good news about Him is told, all over the world (Mark 14:9). And here we are, two thousand years later, still telling her story!

Mary gave Jesus her very best, because He was worth it. What would it look like for us to love Jesus like Mary did?

Read it in your Bible: John 12:1–8; Mark 14:3–9

Dear Jesus, you are worth more than anything. Help me to love you with all my heart, like Mary did, and to give you my very best. Amen.

study_questions.question: What did Mary pour over Jesus’ feet, and how did she dry them?
study_questions.answer: Very expensive perfume made from nard, worth about a year’s wages, and she wiped His feet with her hair.

study_questions.question: Why did Judas complain, and what was the real reason?
study_questions.answer: He said the perfume should have been sold and the money given to the poor. But really, he was a thief who stole from the money bag.

study_questions.question: Mary gave Jesus the most precious thing she had. What is something precious you could give to Jesus?
study_questions.answer: It might be our time, our love, our worship, or something we care about. Jesus is worth our very best.

fields.title: The King on a Donkey
fields.body_html:
“Hosanna to the Son of David! ... Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!” — Matthew 21:9

The next day, Jesus and His disciples set off for Jerusalem. It was nearly time for the Passover festival, and the roads were crowded with people going up to the city.

When they came near Jerusalem, Jesus sent two of His disciples ahead. “Go into the village in front of you,” He said. “As soon as you go in, you’ll find a donkey tied there, with her colt beside her. Untie them and bring them to Me. If anyone asks what you’re doing, just say, ‘The Lord needs them.’”

The disciples went, and found everything just as Jesus had said. They brought the donkey and the colt, and put their cloaks on them, and Jesus sat on them.

Then Jesus rode towards Jerusalem.

A huge crowd gathered. People spread their cloaks on the road in front of Him, like a carpet for a king. Others cut branches from the palm trees and laid them on the road and waved them in the air.

And the crowds in front of Jesus and behind Him were shouting:

“Hosanna to the Son of David!
Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!
Hosanna in the highest!”

“Hosanna” means “Save us now!” The people were welcoming Jesus as the King from David’s family, the Saviour they had been waiting for.

When Jesus rode into Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred up. “Who is this?” people asked.

“This is Jesus, the prophet from Nazareth in Galilee,” the crowds answered.

Kings usually rode into cities on great war horses, with soldiers marching behind them. But Jesus came on a donkey, a humble animal, the kind ordinary people rode. He wasn’t coming to fight the Romans. He was a different kind of King, a gentle King, coming in peace.

The crowds cheered for Jesus that day. But many of them wanted Him to be a King who would fight their enemies and make them powerful. They didn’t understand what kind of King He really was. And in just a few days, some of the same people would be shouting something very different.

We remember this day every year. It’s called Palm Sunday, because of the palm branches the people waved.

The promise kept: Matthew tells us this happened to keep the promise God gave through the prophet Zechariah: “See, your King comes to you, gentle and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey” (Matthew 21:5).

Read it in your Bible: Matthew 21:1–11; John 12:12–16

Hosanna! Thank you, Jesus, that you are the King who came in peace. You are my King. Please help me to welcome you and follow you every day. Amen.

study_questions.question: What did the crowds do and shout when Jesus rode into Jerusalem?
study_questions.answer: They spread their cloaks and palm branches on the road and shouted, “Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!”

study_questions.question: Why did Jesus ride on a donkey, not a war horse?
study_questions.answer: To show He was a gentle King who came in peace, not to fight, just as the prophet Zechariah had promised.

study_questions.question: What does “Hosanna” mean, and why was it a good thing to shout to Jesus?
study_questions.answer: It means “Save us now!” Jesus really did come to save, though not in the way most people expected.

fields.title: Children Singing in the Temple
fields.body_html:
“From the mouths of children and infants You have ordained praise.” — Matthew 21:16

When Jesus came into Jerusalem, He went to the temple, the great house of God.

But the temple courts didn’t look like a place for praying. They looked like a noisy market. People were buying and selling animals for sacrifices. Money changers sat at tables, swapping people’s money for the special coins used in the temple, and often cheating them. There was shouting and bargaining everywhere.

Jesus drove out everyone who was buying and selling. He turned over the tables of the money changers and the seats of the people selling doves.

“It is written,” said Jesus, “‘My house will be called a house of prayer.’ But you are making it a den of robbers!”

Then something beautiful happened. Blind people and people who couldn’t walk came to Jesus in the temple. And He healed them.

And children were running about in the temple courts, shouting the same thing the crowds had shouted the day before: “Hosanna to the Son of David!”

But the chief priests and teachers of the law were furious. They saw the wonderful things Jesus was doing, and they heard the children praising Him, and they were angry.

“Do You hear what these children are saying?” they asked Jesus.

“Yes,” Jesus answered. “Haven’t you ever read, ‘From the mouths of children and infants You have ordained praise’?”

The important religious leaders didn’t praise Jesus. But the children did! The children could see what the grown-ups couldn’t. And Jesus was glad to hear them.

Your praise matters to Jesus. You don’t have to be a grown-up, or important, or clever, to praise Him. God loves to hear children praise Him.

But the chief priests and teachers of the law began looking for a way to kill Jesus. They were afraid of Him, because the whole crowd was amazed at His teaching. Every day that week Jesus taught in the temple, and every night He went out of the city to stay in Bethany.

The promise kept: Jesus answered the chief priests with words from Psalm 8: “From the mouths of children and infants You have ordained praise” (Matthew 21:16). And He called the temple a house of prayer, as God had said through Isaiah (Isaiah 56:7).

Read it in your Bible: Matthew 21:12–17

Dear Jesus, thank you that you love to hear children praise you. Hosanna to the Son of David! Please help me to praise you with my whole heart. Amen.

study_questions.question: What was wrong with the temple when Jesus arrived?
study_questions.answer: It had become a noisy market, with people buying and selling and money changers cheating people, instead of a house of prayer.

study_questions.question: What were the children shouting in the temple?
study_questions.answer: “Hosanna to the Son of David!”

study_questions.question: The children praised Jesus when the grown-up leaders didn’t. How could you praise Jesus today?
study_questions.answer: By singing to Him, thanking Him in prayer, telling Him how great He is, or telling someone else about Him.

fields.title: The Widow’s Two Coins
fields.body_html:
“This poor widow has put more than all the others into the treasury.” — Mark 12:43

During that last week, Jesus taught every day in the temple courts. One day He sat down opposite the place where people put their money offerings, and He watched the crowd putting their gifts into the treasury.

Many rich people came and threw in large amounts of money. Some of them made sure everyone could see how much they were giving.

Then a poor widow came along. She was a woman whose husband had died, and she had very little money. She put in two very small copper coins, the smallest coins there were. Together they were worth hardly anything at all.

Jesus called His disciples over to Him.

“I tell you the truth,” Jesus said, “this poor widow has put more into the treasury than all the others. They all gave out of their riches, the money they had left over. But she, out of her poverty, put in everything she had, all she had to live on.”

The rich people’s gifts looked much bigger. They made a much louder noise when they dropped into the box. People probably noticed them and were impressed.

Nobody noticed the widow. Nobody except Jesus.

And Jesus saw what nobody else saw. The rich people still had plenty left over after they gave. But the widow had given everything. She trusted God to look after her, even when she had nothing left.

God doesn’t measure our gifts the way people do. He doesn’t ask, “How much did you give?” He asks, “How much did you keep?” And He looks at our hearts. He sees whether we are giving out of love and trust, or just to look good.

You might think you don’t have much to give to God. But God sees everything you give Him, even the smallest gift. If you give with a loving heart, it’s worth more to Him than all the riches in the world.

And in just a few days, Jesus would do the same as the widow, only far, far more. He would give everything He had, His own life, for us.

Read it in your Bible: Mark 12:41–44

Dear Jesus, thank you that you see even the smallest gift. Help me to give to you with a loving and trusting heart, not to show off. Amen.

study_questions.question: What did the widow put into the treasury?
study_questions.answer: Two very small copper coins, which was everything she had to live on.

study_questions.question: Why did Jesus say she had given more than all the rich people?
study_questions.answer: Because they gave out of what they had left over, but she gave everything she had, trusting God to care for her.

study_questions.question: What could you give to God, even if it seems small?
study_questions.answer: Some of your money, your time, your help, or your kindness. God sees every gift and loves it when we give with a loving heart.

fields.body_text: “This poor widow has put more than all the others into the treasury.” — Mark 12:43 During that last week, Jesus taught every day in the temple courts. One day He sat down opposite the place where people put their money offerings, and He watched the crowd putting their gifts into the treasury. Many rich people came and threw in large amounts of money. Some of them made sure everyone could see how much they were giving. Then a poor widow came along. She was a woman whose husband had died, and she had very little money. She put in two very small copper coins, the smallest coins there were. Together they were worth hardly anything at all. Jesus called His disciples over to Him. “I tell you the truth,” Jesus said, “this poor widow has put more into the treasury than all the others. They all gave out of their riches, the money they had left over. But she, out of her poverty, put in everything she had, all she had to live on.” The rich people’s gifts looked much bigger. They made a much louder noise when they dropped into the box. People probably noticed them and were impressed. Nobody noticed the widow. Nobody except Jesus. And Jesus saw what nobody else saw. The rich people still had plenty left over after they gave. But the widow had given everything. She trusted God to look after her, even when she had nothing left. God doesn’t measure our gifts the way people do. He doesn’t ask, “How much did you give?” He asks, “How much did you keep?” And He looks at our hearts. He sees whether we are giving out of love and trust, or just to look good. You might think you don’t have much to give to God. But God sees everything you give Him, even the smallest gift. If you give with a loving heart, it’s worth more to Him than all the riches in the world. And in just a few days, Jesus would do the same as the widow, only far, far more. He would give everything He had, His own life, for us. Read it in your Bible: Mark 12:41–44 Dear Jesus, thank you that you see even the smallest gift. Help me to give to you with a loving and trusting heart, not to show off. Amen.

fields.title: Jesus Washes Their Feet
fields.body_html:
“As I have loved you, so you also must love one another.” — John 13:34

It was the evening before the Passover. Jesus and His twelve disciples gathered in an upstairs room in Jerusalem for a special meal together. Jesus knew that the time had come for Him to leave this world and go back to the Father. And He loved His disciples to the very end.

In those days people walked everywhere in sandals, on dusty, dirty roads. So when guests came for a meal, a servant would wash their feet. It was the lowest, dirtiest job in the house.

But there was no servant in the room that night. And none of the disciples offered to do it.

So Jesus got up from the table. He took off His outer robe and wrapped a towel around His waist. He poured water into a bowl. And He began to wash His disciples’ feet, and dry them with the towel.

Jesus, the King of kings, the Son of God, knelt down on the floor like a servant and washed their dirty feet.

When He came to Simon Peter, Peter said, “Lord, are You going to wash my feet?”

“You don’t understand now what I am doing,” said Jesus, “but later you will understand.”

“No!” said Peter. “You will never wash my feet!”

“Unless I wash you,” said Jesus, “you can’t belong to Me.”

“Then, Lord,” said Peter, “don’t wash just my feet. Wash my hands and my head too!”

When Jesus had finished washing their feet, He put His robe back on and sat down again.

“Do you understand what I have done for you?” He asked them. “You call Me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, because that is what I am. Now that I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also should wash one another’s feet. I have given you an example, so that you should do as I have done for you.”

Later that evening, Jesus said, “A new commandment I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you also must love one another. This is how everyone will know that you are My disciples: if you love one another.”

Jesus wasn’t too great to do the lowliest job. He served His friends. And He showed us that real greatness isn’t about being served. It’s about serving other people, out of love.

Read it in your Bible: John 13:1–17, 34–35

Dear Jesus, thank you that you came to serve, not to be served. Help me to love other people the way you love me, and to serve them, even when it’s a job nobody wants to do. Amen.

study_questions.question: Why was washing feet such a lowly job?
study_questions.answer: Because people walked everywhere in sandals on dirty roads, and it was usually the job of the lowest servant in the house.

study_questions.question: What did Jesus say His disciples should do after He washed their feet?
study_questions.answer: Wash one another’s feet, which means serve one another, following His example.

study_questions.question: Jesus said people would know we are His disciples if we love one another. What is a “foot-washing” job you could do for someone at home?
study_questions.answer: Think of a helpful job nobody likes, such as tidying up, helping a brother or sister, or serving a meal, and do it out of love.

fields.title: The Last Supper
fields.body_html:
“This is My body, given for you; do this in remembrance of Me.” — Luke 22:19

It was the night of the Passover meal. All over Jerusalem, families were eating the Passover lamb, remembering the night God rescued His people from Egypt, when the blood on the doorposts kept them safe.

Jesus sat at the table with His twelve disciples. “I have really wanted to eat this Passover with you before I suffer,” He told them.

While they were eating, Jesus said something that upset them all. “I tell you the truth, one of you will betray Me.”

The disciples were very sad. They looked at each other. “Surely not I, Lord?” each one said.

Judas Iscariot had already gone to the chief priests and agreed to hand Jesus over to them, for thirty silver coins. Now Judas got up and went out into the night.

Then Jesus took some bread. He gave thanks to God, broke it, and gave it to His disciples. “This is My body, given for you,” He said. “Do this in remembrance of Me.”

After supper He took the cup of wine. “This cup is the new covenant in My blood,” He said, “which is poured out for you, for the forgiveness of sins.”

The disciples didn’t fully understand. But Jesus was telling them what was about to happen. His body would be broken. His blood would be poured out. Like the Passover lamb, He would die so that His people would be safe.

The bread and the wine would help them remember. And Christians all over the world still do this today. We call it Communion, or the Lord’s Supper. When we eat the bread and drink from the cup, we remember Jesus, who gave His body and His blood for us.

Then Jesus told Peter something sad. “Peter, before the rooster crows tonight, you will say three times that you don’t know Me.”

“Lord,” said Peter, “I’m ready to go to prison with You, and even to die with You!”

But Jesus knew what would happen.

When they had sung a hymn together, they went out into the night, to the Mount of Olives.

The promise kept: Jesus is “our Passover lamb” (1 Corinthians 5:7). And when He spoke of “the new covenant”, He meant the promise God made through the prophet Jeremiah: “the days are coming ... when I will make a new covenant,” a promise to forgive sins and remember them no more (Hebrews 8:8; Jeremiah 31:34).

Read it in your Bible: Luke 22:7–23, 31–34; Matthew 26:17–30

Dear Jesus, thank you that you gave your body and your blood for me. Help me always to remember what you did for me. Amen.

study_questions.question: What festival were Jesus and His disciples celebrating, and what did it remember?
study_questions.answer: The Passover, which remembered how God rescued His people from Egypt, when the blood of the lamb on their doorposts kept them safe.

study_questions.question: What did Jesus say about the bread and the cup?
study_questions.answer: That the bread was His body, given for them, and the cup was the new covenant in His blood, poured out for the forgiveness of sins.

study_questions.question: Why do Christians still share bread and wine today?
study_questions.answer: To remember Jesus and how He gave His life for us, just as He asked. (If your church shares Communion, this is a good time to talk about what it means.)

fields.title: Praying in the Garden
fields.body_html:
“Yet not what I will, but what You will.” — Mark 14:36

After the supper, Jesus and His disciples went out to a garden of olive trees called Gethsemane. It was late at night.

“Sit here while I pray,” Jesus told most of the disciples. He took Peter and James and John with Him, a little further into the garden.

Then Jesus began to be very troubled and full of sorrow. “My soul is so sad, I feel I could die,” He told them. “Stay here and keep watch.”

Jesus knew what was about to happen. He knew that soon He would be arrested, and that He would suffer and die. And He knew that on the cross He would carry the sin of the whole world. It was the hardest thing anyone has ever had to do.

Jesus went a little further and fell to the ground and prayed. “Abba, Father,” He prayed. Abba is the word a child uses for “Dad”. “Everything is possible for You. Please take this cup of suffering away from Me. Yet not what I want, but what You want.”

Then Jesus came back to the three disciples. And they were asleep!

“Simon, are you asleep?” Jesus said to Peter. “Couldn’t you keep watch for one hour? Watch and pray, so that you will not fall into temptation. The spirit is willing, but the body is weak.”

Jesus went away again and prayed the same prayer. When He came back, the disciples were asleep again. Their eyes were so heavy, they didn’t know what to say to Him.

A third time Jesus went away and prayed. Luke tells us that an angel from heaven came and gave Him strength. And Jesus prayed even harder, in such anguish that His sweat was like drops of blood falling to the ground.

When Jesus came back the third time, He said, “Are you still sleeping and resting? Enough! The time has come. Get up! Let’s go! Look, here comes the one who is betraying Me!”

In the garden, Jesus didn’t want to suffer. He was a real man, and He felt real sorrow and fear. But He wanted to do His Father’s will even more. “Not what I want, but what You want.” He chose to go to the cross, because He loved His Father, and He loved us.

Read it in your Bible: Mark 14:32–42; Luke 22:39–46

Dear Jesus, thank you that you chose to do your Father’s will, even though it was so hard. When I have to do something hard, help me to pray, “Not what I want, but what you want.” Amen.

study_questions.question: What did Jesus pray in the garden?
study_questions.answer: “Abba, Father, everything is possible for You. Please take this cup of suffering away from Me. Yet not what I want, but what You want.”

study_questions.question: What were Peter, James and John doing while Jesus prayed?
study_questions.answer: They kept falling asleep, even though Jesus asked them to watch and pray with Him.

study_questions.question: Jesus felt sad and afraid, but He still obeyed His Father. What does that teach us when we have to do something hard?
study_questions.answer: That it’s all right to tell God how we really feel, and to ask Him for help, while trusting that His way is best.

fields.title: Arrested at Night
fields.body_html:
“Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?” — John 18:11

While Jesus was still speaking, a crowd came into the garden, carrying torches and lanterns and swords and clubs. They had been sent by the chief priests. And leading them was Judas, one of Jesus’ own twelve disciples.

Judas had told them, “The one I kiss is the man you want. Arrest Him.” It was dark, and he wanted to make sure they took the right person.

Judas walked straight up to Jesus. “Greetings, Teacher!” he said, and kissed Him.

“Judas,” said Jesus, “are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?” A kiss was a sign of friendship. Judas was using it to betray his friend.

Jesus knew everything that was going to happen to Him. He stepped forward. “Who are you looking for?” He asked.

“Jesus of Nazareth,” they answered.

“I am He,” said Jesus.

And when Jesus said, “I am He,” they all stepped back and fell to the ground! Even the soldiers couldn’t stand before Him. Nobody was taking Jesus’ life from Him. He was giving it.

“I told you that I am He,” said Jesus. “If you are looking for Me, then let these men go.” Even now, Jesus was protecting His friends.

Then Peter pulled out a sword and swung it at the high priest’s servant, a man called Malchus, and cut off his right ear!

“Put your sword away!” Jesus said to Peter. “Shall I not drink the cup My Father has given Me?”

And Jesus touched the man’s ear and healed him. Even while He was being arrested, Jesus was kind to one of the men who had come to arrest Him.

Then the soldiers seized Jesus and tied Him up.

“Am I leading a rebellion,” Jesus said to the crowd, “that you have come out with swords and clubs to arrest Me? Every day I was with you in the temple courts, and you didn’t lay a hand on Me. But this is your hour, when darkness reigns.”

And then all the disciples left Him and ran away.

They had promised to stay with Jesus, even if it meant dying with Him. But when the soldiers came, they were too frightened. Jesus was left alone.

They led Jesus away into the night, to the house of the high priest.

Jesus could have called on His Father to send armies of angels to rescue Him (Matthew 26:53). But He didn’t. He let Himself be arrested. He was choosing to go to the cross, to rescue us.

Read it in your Bible: John 18:1–12; Luke 22:47–53

Dear Jesus, thank you that you chose to give your life for us. Thank you that you were kind even to the people who came to arrest you. Help me to be kind to people who are unkind to me. Amen.

study_questions.question: How did Judas show the soldiers which one was Jesus?
study_questions.answer: He greeted Jesus with a kiss, which was usually a sign of friendship.

study_questions.question: What did Jesus do when Peter cut off the servant’s ear?
study_questions.answer: He told Peter to put his sword away, and He touched the man’s ear and healed him.

study_questions.question: When Jesus said, “I am He,” the soldiers fell to the ground. What does that tell us?
study_questions.answer: That Jesus had all the power, and nobody could take His life from Him. He chose to give it, because He loved us.

fields.title: Peter’s Three Denials
fields.body_html:
“And the Lord turned and looked at Peter.” — Luke 22:61

The soldiers took Jesus to the high priest’s house. Peter had run away with the others. But now he followed, a long way behind, and crept into the courtyard of the house.

It was cold that night. Some people had lit a fire in the middle of the courtyard, and they were sitting around it to keep warm. Peter sat down with them.

A servant girl saw Peter sitting there in the firelight. She looked closely at him. “This man was with Jesus,” she said.

But Peter said, “Woman, I don’t know Him!”

A little later, someone else saw him. “You’re one of them too!”

“Man, I am not!” said Peter.

About an hour later, another man said firmly, “This man was definitely with Jesus. He’s from Galilee, like Jesus.” People could tell by the way Peter spoke.

“Man, I don’t know what you’re talking about!” said Peter.

And just as he was speaking, a rooster crowed.

At that moment, the Lord turned and looked straight at Peter.

And Peter remembered what Jesus had said to him only a few hours before: “Before the rooster crows today, you will say three times that you don’t know Me.”

Peter went outside and cried and cried.

Peter loved Jesus. He had said he would die for Him. But when he was frightened, he pretended he didn’t even know Him. Three times.

What do you think Jesus’ look was like? Was it angry? The Bible doesn’t tell us. But Jesus knew this would happen, and He still loved Peter. Earlier that evening He had said to him, “I have prayed for you, Simon, that your faith will not fail. And when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32).

Jesus knew Peter would fail. And He had already prayed for him, and already planned for him to come back.

This isn’t the end of Peter’s story. Later in this book, you’ll see what Jesus did for Peter after this terrible night.

Sometimes we let Jesus down too. We do things we know are wrong. We’re too scared to stand up for Him. But Jesus doesn’t give up on us, just as He didn’t give up on Peter.

Read it in your Bible: Luke 22:31–34, 54–62

Dear Jesus, I am sorry for the times I have let you down. Thank you that you never stop loving me, and that you pray for me. Please make me brave to stand up for you. Amen.

study_questions.question: How many times did Peter say he didn’t know Jesus?
study_questions.answer: Three times, to three different people in the high priest’s courtyard.

study_questions.question: What happened right after the third time?
study_questions.answer: A rooster crowed, Jesus turned and looked at Peter, and Peter remembered what Jesus had said. He went outside and cried bitterly.

study_questions.question: Jesus knew Peter would fail, and still loved him. How does that help us when we let Jesus down?
study_questions.answer: It shows that Jesus doesn’t give up on us. We can tell Him we’re sorry and know He still loves us and wants us back.

fields.title: Jesus and Pilate
fields.body_html:
“For this reason I was born and have come into the world, to testify to the truth.” — John 18:37

All through that night, the religious leaders questioned Jesus. They found people to tell lies about Him. But their stories didn’t agree.

At last the high priest asked Him, “Are You the Christ, the Son of God?”

“I am,” said Jesus.

“He has spoken against God!” the high priest shouted. And they decided that Jesus must die.

But only the Roman governor could order someone to be put to death. So early in the morning, they took Jesus to the governor, a man called Pontius Pilate.

“Are You the King of the Jews?” Pilate asked Jesus.

“My kingdom is not of this world,” said Jesus. “If it were, My servants would fight to stop My arrest. But My kingdom is from another place.”

“So You are a king, then!” said Pilate.

“You say that I am a king,” Jesus answered. “For this reason I was born, and came into the world: to tell people the truth. Everyone who belongs to the truth listens to Me.”

“What is truth?” said Pilate.

Then Pilate went out to the crowd. “I find nothing wrong with this man,” he said. “It’s your custom for me to set one prisoner free at Passover time. Do you want me to set free the King of the Jews?”

But the chief priests had stirred up the crowd. “No, not Him!” they shouted. “Give us Barabbas!” Barabbas was a man who had led a violent rebellion.

Then Pilate had Jesus whipped. The soldiers twisted some thorny branches into a crown and pushed it onto His head. They dressed Him in a purple robe, the colour kings wore. And they made fun of Him. “Hail, King of the Jews!” they jeered, and they hit Him.

Pilate brought Jesus out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe. “Here is the man!” said Pilate.

When the chief priests saw Him, they shouted, “Crucify Him! Crucify Him!”

“I find nothing wrong with Him,” Pilate said again.

fields.title: The Cross
fields.body_html:
“Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” — Luke 23:34

The soldiers led Jesus away to be crucified. He had been up all night, and He had been beaten and whipped. As they went, the soldiers grabbed a man called Simon from Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, and made him carry the heavy wooden cross behind Jesus.

They came to a hill outside the city called the Place of the Skull, or Golgotha. And there the soldiers nailed Jesus to the cross, and lifted it up.

Two criminals were crucified with Him, one on His right and one on His left.

And Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

Even while they were hurting Him, Jesus prayed for the people who were doing it.

Pilate had a sign put on the cross above Jesus’ head. It said: JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS. It was written in three languages, so that everyone could read it.

The soldiers sat down at the foot of the cross and gambled to see who would get Jesus’ clothes.

People walking past laughed at Jesus and shouted insults. “He saved other people,” the religious leaders sneered. “Let Him save Himself, if He is the Christ!” The soldiers made fun of Him too.

One of the criminals hanging beside Jesus joined in. “Aren’t You the Christ? Save Yourself, and us!”

But the other criminal told him off. “Don’t you fear God?” he said. “We deserve to be punished for what we did. But this man has done nothing wrong.”

Then he said, “Jesus, remember me when You come into Your kingdom.”

And Jesus said to him, “I tell you the truth, today you will be with Me in paradise.”

That man had done terrible things. He couldn’t go to church, or be baptised, or do anything good to make up for what he had done. He was dying. All he could do was turn to Jesus and trust Him. And that was enough. Jesus promised that he would be with Him in paradise that very day.

Near the cross stood Jesus’ mother, Mary, and some other women, and the disciple John. Jesus saw His mother there. “Woman, here is your son,” He said to her, about John. And to John He said, “Here is your mother.” Even on the cross, Jesus made sure His mother would be looked after. From that day, John took Mary into his home.

The people who said “Save Yourself!” didn’t understand. Jesus could have saved Himself. But if He saved Himself, He couldn’t save us.

The promise kept: John tells us that when the soldiers gambled for Jesus’ clothes, it kept the words of Psalm 22, written a thousand years before: “They divided My garments among them, and cast lots for My clothing” (John 19:24).

Read it in your Bible: Luke 23:26–43; John 19:17–27

Dear Jesus, thank you that you stayed on the cross to save us, and that you forgave the people who hurt you. Jesus, remember me. Amen.

study_questions.question: What did Jesus pray for the people who crucified Him?
study_questions.answer: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

study_questions.question: What did Jesus promise the criminal who asked Him to remember him?
study_questions.answer: “Today you will be with Me in paradise.”

study_questions.question: The criminal couldn’t do anything good to make up for his wrongs. He just trusted Jesus. What does that teach us about how people are saved?
study_questions.answer: That we are saved by trusting Jesus, not by being good enough. It’s never too late to turn to Him. (This chapter is told simply; let your child ask whatever they want, and it’s fine to say “Jesus suffered because He loves us.”)

fields.title: “It Is Finished”
fields.body_html:
“He said, ‘It is finished.’ And bowing His head, He yielded up His spirit.” — John 19:30

At about twelve o’clock, in the middle of the day, darkness came over the whole land. For three hours, from noon until three o’clock in the afternoon, it was as dark as night.

At about three o’clock, Jesus cried out in a loud voice, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”

On the cross, Jesus was carrying the sin of the whole world: all the wrong things that everyone has ever done. Sin separates people from God. And for the first time ever, Jesus felt that separation. He was taking the punishment that we deserved, so that we would never have to be separated from God.

Then Jesus said, “I am thirsty.” Someone dipped a sponge in sour wine, put it on a stick, and lifted it up to His mouth.

When Jesus had received the drink, He said, “It is finished!”

Then He called out in a loud voice, “Father, into Your hands I commit My spirit.” And He bowed His head, and died.

“It is finished!” wasn’t a cry of defeat. It was a shout of victory. Jesus had done everything He came to do. The work of rescuing us was complete. Nothing more needed to be added. The price for our sins was fully paid.

At that very moment, something amazing happened in the temple. The temple had a huge, thick curtain that hung in front of the Most Holy Place, the room where God’s presence was. Only the high priest could go in there, once a year. The curtain showed that sin kept people out of God’s presence.

When Jesus died, that curtain was torn in two, from top to bottom! It was torn from the top, as if God Himself had ripped it. The way into God’s presence was open. Because of Jesus, anyone can come to God now.

The earth shook, and rocks split apart.

A Roman centurion was standing in front of the cross, the officer in charge of the soldiers who crucified Jesus. When he saw how Jesus died, he said, “Surely this man was the Son of God!”

The women who had followed Jesus from Galilee were watching from a distance, with broken hearts.

Jesus’ friends thought it was all over. They thought it was the end of everything.

But it was only Friday.

The promise kept: Jesus’ cry “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” (Matthew 27:46) were the first words of Psalm 22, the same psalm that spoke of His clothes being divided. And John tells us that not one of Jesus’ bones was broken, just like the Passover lamb’s (John 19:36; Exodus 12:46).

Read it in your Bible: John 19:28–30; Mark 15:33–41; Luke 23:44–49

Dear Jesus, thank you that you finished everything needed to rescue me. Thank you that because of you, the way to God is open, and I can come to Him. Amen.

study_questions.question: What happened to the curtain in the temple when Jesus died, and what does it mean?
study_questions.answer: It was torn in two from top to bottom. It means that because of Jesus, the way into God’s presence is open to everyone.

study_questions.question: What did Jesus mean when He said, “It is finished”?
study_questions.answer: That He had completed everything He came to do. The price for our sins was fully paid.

study_questions.question: How does it make you feel to know that Jesus died for you?
study_questions.answer: Let your child answer. It’s a big thing to take in. You can thank Jesus together, and remember that the story isn’t over yet.

fields.title: Laid in the Tomb
fields.body_html:
“Then he rolled a great stone across the entrance to the tomb and went away.” — Matthew 27:60

It was Friday evening, and soon the Sabbath would begin, the day of rest, when no one could work. Jesus’ body couldn’t be left on the cross.

There was a rich man called Joseph, from a town called Arimathea. He was a member of the council of Jewish leaders, but he had not agreed with their plan to kill Jesus. Joseph was a follower of Jesus, but he had kept it secret, because he was afraid.

But now Joseph was brave. He went to Pilate and asked if he could have Jesus’ body. Pilate said yes.

Another leader came too: Nicodemus, the man who had once come to Jesus at night. He brought about seventy-five pounds of spices, myrrh and aloes, to put on Jesus’ body. That was a gift fit for a king.

Joseph and Nicodemus took Jesus’ body down from the cross. They wrapped it with the spices in strips of clean linen cloth. And they laid it in Joseph’s own new tomb, which had been cut out of the rock in a garden nearby. Nobody had ever been laid in it before.

Then Joseph rolled a huge stone across the entrance to the tomb, and went away.

Mary Magdalene and some of the other women who loved Jesus were there, sitting opposite the tomb, watching. They saw exactly where Jesus’ body was laid. Then they went home to prepare more spices, so that they could come back after the Sabbath.

The next day, the chief priests and Pharisees went to Pilate. “Sir,” they said, “we remember that while He was still alive, that deceiver said, ‘After three days I will rise again.’ So give orders for the tomb to be made secure until the third day. Otherwise His disciples may come and steal the body, and tell the people He has been raised from the dead.”

“Take a guard,” said Pilate. “Go and make the tomb as secure as you can.”

So they went and sealed the stone, and put soldiers on guard outside the tomb.

That Saturday was the saddest, quietest day. Jesus’ friends hid away, heartbroken and afraid. Everything they had hoped for seemed to be lying dead in that tomb, behind the great stone, with soldiers standing guard.

But Jesus had said He would rise on the third day. The chief priests remembered. His friends had forgotten.

Read it in your Bible: Matthew 27:57–66; John 19:38–42

Dear Jesus, thank you that even on the saddest days, you have not forgotten your promises. When I am sad, help me to remember that you are still in charge. Amen.

study_questions.question: Who took care of Jesus’ body after He died?
study_questions.answer: Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus, who wrapped it in linen with spices and laid it in Joseph’s new tomb.

study_questions.question: Why did the chief priests ask Pilate to put guards at the tomb?
study_questions.answer: Because they remembered Jesus had said He would rise again after three days, and they wanted to stop anyone stealing the body.

study_questions.question: Joseph had been a secret follower of Jesus, but he became brave. When might you need to be brave to show you follow Jesus?
study_questions.answer: Perhaps when friends laugh at church or prayer, or when it’s easier to stay quiet. Like Joseph, we can ask God to make us brave.

fields.title: He Is Risen!
fields.body_html:
“He is not here; He has risen, just as He said!” — Matthew 28:6

Very early on Sunday morning, the first day of the week, while it was still dark, some women set off for the tomb. Mary Magdalene was there, and another Mary, and some others. They were carrying the spices they had prepared, to put on Jesus’ body.

“Who will roll the stone away from the entrance for us?” they asked each other. The stone was very big, much too heavy for them to move.

But early that morning there had been a great earthquake. An angel of the Lord had come down from heaven, rolled back the stone, and sat on it! His face shone like lightning, and his clothes were as white as snow. The guards were so afraid of him that they shook and fell down like dead men.

When the women arrived, they looked up and saw that the stone had already been rolled away!

They went into the tomb. But Jesus’ body wasn’t there.

They didn’t know what to think. Suddenly two men in shining clothes were standing beside them. The women were terrified and bowed down with their faces to the ground.

“Why do you look for the living among the dead?” the angels asked. “He is not here. He has risen! Remember how He told you, while He was still in Galilee, that He must be handed over to sinful men, and be crucified, and on the third day rise again?”

Then they remembered Jesus’ words.

“Do not be afraid,” said the angel. “I know that you are looking for Jesus, who was crucified. He is not here. He has risen, just as He said! Come and see the place where He lay. Then go quickly and tell His disciples: ‘He has risen from the dead, and He is going ahead of you into Galilee. There you will see Him.’”

The women hurried away from the tomb, afraid and yet filled with great joy, and ran to tell the disciples.

And on the way, suddenly, Jesus met them! “Greetings!” He said. They came to Him, held on to His feet, and worshipped Him.

“Don’t be afraid,” said Jesus. “Go and tell My brothers to go to Galilee. They will see Me there.”

The women told the disciples everything. But at first the disciples didn’t believe them. It sounded like nonsense!

Jesus is alive! He really died, but He didn’t stay dead. On the third day, just as He had promised, He rose from the dead. Death couldn’t hold Him.

That means Jesus really did defeat sin and death. He is stronger than death. And everyone who trusts in Him will live for ever with Him too.

This is the best news in the whole world. It’s why Christians celebrate Easter. Jesus is risen!

Read it in your Bible: Matthew 28:1–10; Luke 24:1–12

Jesus, you are alive! Thank you that you rose from the dead, just as you promised. Thank you that you have beaten death, and that I can live for ever with you. Hallelujah! Amen.

study_questions.answer: The stone had been rolled away, and Jesus’ body wasn’t there. Angels told them, “He is not here; He has risen, just as He said!”

study_questions.question: Who did the women meet on the way to tell the disciples?
study_questions.answer: Jesus Himself! They held on to His feet and worshipped Him.

study_questions.question: Why is Jesus rising from the dead the best news in the world?
study_questions.answer: Because it shows that Jesus really defeated sin and death, and everyone who trusts Him will live for ever with Him.

fields.title: Mary in the Garden
fields.body_html:
“Jesus said to her, ‘Mary.’” — John 20:16

When Mary Magdalene first saw that the stone had been rolled away from the tomb, she ran to find Peter and John. “They have taken the Lord out of the tomb,” she cried, “and we don’t know where they have put Him!”

Peter and John ran to the tomb. John ran faster and got there first. He bent down and looked in, and saw the strips of linen lying there. Then Peter arrived and went straight in. He saw the linen strips lying there, and the cloth that had been around Jesus’ head, folded up by itself. Then John went in too. He saw, and he believed. Then they went back home.

But Mary stayed outside the tomb, crying.

As she cried, she bent over to look into the tomb. And she saw two angels in white, sitting where Jesus’ body had been, one at the head and one at the foot.

“Woman, why are you crying?” they asked her.

“They have taken my Lord away,” she said, “and I don’t know where they have put Him.”

Then she turned around, and saw Jesus standing there. But she didn’t know it was Jesus.

“Woman, why are you crying?” He asked. “Who are you looking for?”

She thought He was the gardener. “Sir,” she said, “if you have carried Him away, tell me where you have put Him, and I will go and get Him.”

Then Jesus said to her, “Mary.”

Just one word. Her name. And as soon as she heard Him say her name, she knew!

She turned towards Him and cried out, “Rabboni!” which means “Teacher”.

Mary must have grabbed hold of Him and not wanted to let go. “Don’t hold on to Me,” Jesus said gently, “for I have not yet gone back to the Father. Go instead to My brothers and tell them, ‘I am going back to My Father and your Father, to My God and your God.’”

So Mary Magdalene went to the disciples with the news. “I have seen the Lord!” she told them. And she told them everything He had said.

Mary was the very first person to see Jesus after He rose from the dead. Jesus had once set her free from great trouble (Luke 8:2), and she had followed Him ever since. She had stood near the cross. She had watched where He was buried. She had come in the dark to the tomb. And now she was the first to see Him alive, and the first to tell the good news.

Jesus is the Good Shepherd, who calls His sheep by name. He knew Mary’s name, and He knows yours too.

Read it in your Bible: John 20:1–18

Dear Jesus, thank you that you know my name. Thank you that you are alive, and that you came to Mary when she was crying. I want to tell people, like Mary did, “I have seen the Lord!” Amen.

study_questions.question: Who did Mary think Jesus was when she first saw Him?
study_questions.answer: She thought He was the gardener.

study_questions.question: How did Mary realise it was Jesus?
study_questions.answer: He said her name, “Mary”, and as soon as she heard Him say it, she knew Him.

study_questions.question: Jesus knew Mary’s name. How does it feel to know that Jesus knows your name too?
study_questions.answer: Let your child answer. Jesus knows each of us personally and calls us by name, like a shepherd who knows every one of his sheep.

He saw the linen strips lying there, and the cloth that had been around Jesus’ head, folded up by itself. Then John went in too. He saw, and he believed. Then they went back home. But Mary stayed outside the tomb, crying. As she cried, she bent over to look into the tomb. And she saw two angels in white, sitting where Jesus’ body had been, one at the head and one at the foot. “Woman, why are you crying?” they asked her. “They have taken my Lord away,” she said, “and I don’t know where they have put Him.” Then she turned around, and saw Jesus standing there. But she didn’t know it was Jesus. “Woman, why are you crying?” He asked. “Who are you looking for?” She thought He was the gardener. “Sir,” she said, “if you have carried Him away, tell me where you have put Him, and I will go and get Him.” Then Jesus said to her, “Mary.” Just one word. Her name. And as soon as she heard Him say her name, she knew! She turned towards Him and cried out, “Rabboni!” which means “Teacher”. Mary must have grabbed hold of Him and not wanted to let go. “Don’t hold on to Me,” Jesus said gently, “for I have not yet gone back to the Father. Go instead to My brothers and tell them, ‘I am going back to My Father and your Father, to My God and your God.’” So Mary Magdalene went to the disciples with the news. “I have seen the Lord!” she told them. And she told them everything He had said. Mary was the very first person to see Jesus after He rose from the dead. Jesus had once set her free from great trouble (Luke 8:2), and she had followed Him ever since. She had stood near the cross. She had watched where He was buried. She had come in the dark to the tomb. And now she was the first to see Him alive, and the first to tell the good news. Jesus is the Good Shepherd, who calls His sheep by name. He knew Mary’s name, and He knows yours too. Read it in your Bible: John 20:1–18 Dear Jesus, thank you that you know my name. Thank you that you are alive, and that you came to Mary when she was crying. I want to tell people, like Mary did, “I have seen the Lord!” Amen.

fields.title: The Road to Emmaus
fields.body_html:
“Were not our hearts burning within us as He spoke with us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” — Luke 24:32

That same Sunday, two of Jesus’ followers were walking from Jerusalem to a village called Emmaus, about seven miles away. As they walked, they talked about everything that had happened.

Then Jesus Himself came up and walked along with them. But they didn’t recognise Him.

“What are you talking about as you walk along?” He asked them.

They stopped, and their faces were sad. One of them, called Cleopas, said, “Are You the only visitor to Jerusalem who doesn’t know what has happened there these last few days?”

“What things?” asked Jesus.

“About Jesus of Nazareth,” they said. “He was a prophet, powerful in everything He said and did. But the chief priests and our leaders handed Him over to be killed, and they crucified Him. We had hoped that He was the one who would rescue Israel. And now it’s the third day since all this happened. Some of the women went to His tomb early this morning, and His body wasn’t there! They said they had seen angels, who said He was alive. But nobody has seen Him.”

Then Jesus said, “How foolish you are, and how slow to believe everything the prophets said! Didn’t the Christ have to suffer these things and then enter His glory?”

And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, Jesus explained to them everything the Scriptures said about Himself.

Imagine it. Jesus Himself, walking along the road, taking them through the whole Old Testament! Perhaps He told them about the promise in the garden, that the snake’s head would be crushed. And the lamb God provided on the mountain. And the Passover lamb. And the snake on the pole. And Isaiah’s Servant, who was pierced for our sins. All the stories you have read in these books, Jesus showed them how every one of them pointed to Him.

As they came near Emmaus, Jesus acted as if He was going further. But they begged Him, “Stay with us. It’s nearly evening, and the day is almost over.” So He went in to stay with them.

When they sat down to eat, Jesus took the bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them.

And suddenly their eyes were opened, and they knew Him! It was Jesus! And at that moment, He disappeared from their sight.

“Weren’t our hearts burning inside us,” they said to each other, “while He talked with us on the road and explained the Scriptures to us?”

They got up at once and hurried all the way back to Jerusalem, in the dark. They found the eleven disciples gathered together, and they were saying, “It’s true! The Lord has risen, and He has appeared to Simon!” Then the two told what had happened on the road, and how they had recognised Jesus when He broke the bread.

The promise kept: “Beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, He explained to them what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself” (Luke 24:27). Every “promise kept” in these books, and every “Looking ahead to Jesus”, comes from this: the whole Bible is about Him.

Read it in your Bible: Luke 24:13–35

Dear Jesus, thank you that the whole Bible points to you. Please open my eyes to see you in it, and make my heart burn with love for you, like the friends on the road to Emmaus. Amen.

study_questions.question: Why were the two followers sad as they walked to Emmaus?
study_questions.answer: Because Jesus had been crucified, and they had hoped He was the one who would rescue Israel. They didn’t yet believe He was alive.

study_questions.question: When did they finally recognise Jesus?
study_questions.answer: When He took the bread, gave thanks, broke it and gave it to them.

study_questions.question: Jesus explained how all the Old Testament pointed to Him. Can you think of a story from the earlier books that points to Jesus?
study_questions.answer: For example, the lamb God provided instead of Isaac, the Passover lamb, the snake on the pole, or Jacob’s stairway. Every one shows something about Jesus.

fields.title: “Peace Be with You”
fields.body_html:
“Peace be with you!” — John 20:19

That same Sunday evening, the disciples were together in a room with the doors locked. They were afraid that the religious leaders might come after them next.

While the two friends from Emmaus were telling their story, suddenly Jesus Himself was standing among them.

“Peace be with you!” He said.

The disciples were startled and frightened. They thought they were seeing a ghost!

“Why are you troubled?” Jesus asked. “Why do you have doubts in your hearts? Look at My hands and My feet. It is I Myself! Touch Me and see. A ghost doesn’t have flesh and bones, as you can see I have.”

And He showed them His hands and His feet, and His side, with the marks where the nails and the spear had been.

The disciples were so full of joy and amazement that they could hardly believe it. So Jesus asked them, “Have you got anything here to eat?”

They gave Him a piece of cooked fish, and He took it and ate it in front of them. Ghosts don’t eat fish! Jesus wasn’t a ghost or a spirit. He had a real body. He had really risen from the dead.

Then Jesus said, “Everything that is written about Me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms had to come true.”

And He opened their minds so that they could understand the Scriptures. “This is what is written,” He said. “The Christ will suffer and rise from the dead on the third day. And in His name, the message that people should turn back to God and be forgiven will be preached to all nations, starting from Jerusalem. You are witnesses of these things.”

“Peace be with you,” Jesus said again. “As the Father has sent Me, so I am sending you.”

The disciples had run away and left Jesus alone. Peter had said he didn’t even know Him. They must have wondered whether Jesus would be angry with them. But the first words He said to them were “Peace be with you.”

Jesus didn’t come back to tell them off. He came back to bring them peace, and to send them out with good news.

The promise kept: Jesus said, “Everything must be fulfilled that is written about Me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms” (Luke 24:44). His suffering and His rising again were the promises of the whole Old Testament coming true.

Read it in your Bible: Luke 24:36–49; John 20:19–23

Dear Jesus, thank you for your peace. Thank you that you didn’t come back to tell your friends off, but to forgive them and send them out. Please give me your peace, and send me out too. Amen.

study_questions.question: Why did the disciples think they were seeing a ghost?
study_questions.answer: Because Jesus suddenly appeared in a locked room, and they couldn’t believe He was really alive.

study_questions.question: How did Jesus show them He had a real body?
study_questions.answer: He showed them the marks in His hands, feet and side, told them to touch Him, and ate a piece of fish in front of them.

study_questions.question: The first thing Jesus said to His friends, who had run away, was “Peace be with you.” What does that tell us about Jesus?
study_questions.answer: That He forgives, and that He wants to give us peace, not punish us, when we come back to Him.

fields.title: Thomas Believes
fields.body_html:
“Thomas replied, ‘My Lord and my God!’” — John 20:28

One of the twelve disciples, Thomas, wasn’t with the others when Jesus came on that first Sunday evening.

When Thomas came back, the other disciples told him, “We have seen the Lord!”

But Thomas didn’t believe them. “Unless I see the nail marks in His hands,” he said, “and put my finger where the nails were, and put my hand into His side, I won’t believe it.”

Thomas wasn’t a bad person. He loved Jesus. He had once said he was ready to go and die with Him (John 11:16). But he had seen Jesus die, and it was too hard to believe that He was alive again. He needed to see for himself.

A whole week went by. Thomas must have felt left out, with everyone else so happy and sure.

Eight days later, the disciples were together in the house again, and this time Thomas was with them. The doors were locked. And Jesus came and stood among them.

“Peace be with you!” He said.

Then Jesus turned straight to Thomas. “Put your finger here,” He said, “and look at My hands. Reach out your hand and put it into My side. Stop doubting, and believe.”

Jesus knew exactly what Thomas had said, even though He hadn’t been there to hear it. And He didn’t tell Thomas off. He gave Thomas exactly what he needed.

Thomas didn’t need to touch Jesus after all. He just looked at Him. And he said, “My Lord and my God!”

Thomas, the one who doubted, said something nobody had said so clearly before. Jesus isn’t just a great teacher. He isn’t just a prophet. He is Lord. He is God.

Then Jesus said, “Because you have seen Me, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen Me and yet have believed.”

Who do you think Jesus was talking about? People who would believe in Him without seeing Him with their own eyes. People like you and me! We haven’t seen Jesus the way Thomas did. But we can still believe. And Jesus says we are blessed.

John, who wrote down this story, tells us why he wrote his Gospel: “These are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name.”

Read it in your Bible: John 20:24–31

Dear Jesus, you are my Lord and my God! When I find it hard to believe, please help me. Thank you that you bless people who believe in you without seeing you. Amen.

study_questions.question: What did Thomas say he needed before he would believe?
study_questions.answer: To see the nail marks in Jesus’ hands and put his finger where the nails were and his hand in Jesus’ side.

study_questions.question: What did Thomas say when he saw Jesus?
study_questions.answer: “My Lord and my God!”

study_questions.question: Jesus said, “Blessed are those who have not seen Me and yet have believed.” Who was He talking about?
study_questions.answer: People like us, who believe in Jesus without seeing Him with our own eyes. It’s all right to have questions, like Thomas. Jesus helps us to believe.

fields.title: Breakfast on the Beach
fields.body_html:
“‘Come, have breakfast,’ Jesus said to them.” — John 21:12

Some time later, Peter and some of the other disciples were back in Galilee, by the lake where they used to fish.

“I’m going fishing,” said Peter.

“We’ll come with you,” said the others. So they got into the boat and went out. But all night long, they didn’t catch a thing.

Early in the morning, as the sun was coming up, Jesus was standing on the shore. But the disciples didn’t realise it was Jesus.

“Children,” He called out to them, “haven’t you caught any fish?”

“No,” they answered.

“Throw your net on the right side of the boat,” He said, “and you will find some.”

So they did. And they caught so many fish that they couldn’t pull the net back into the boat!

Do you remember when that happened before? On the day Jesus first called Peter to follow Him, Peter had fished all night and caught nothing too.

John said to Peter, “It’s the Lord!”

As soon as Peter heard that, he pulled on his coat, jumped into the water, and swam to the shore! He couldn’t wait for the boat.

When the others landed, they saw a charcoal fire burning, with fish cooking on it, and some bread. Jesus had made them breakfast!

“Bring some of the fish you’ve just caught,” said Jesus. Peter dragged the net to the shore. It was full of big fish, 153 of them! And even with so many, the net didn’t tear.

“Come and have breakfast,” said Jesus. And He took the bread and gave it to them, and the fish too.

When they had finished eating, Jesus turned to Peter.

“Simon, son of John, do you love Me more than these?”

“Yes, Lord,” said Peter. “You know I love You.”

“Feed My lambs,” said Jesus.

Then Jesus asked again, “Simon, son of John, do you love Me?”

“Yes, Lord, You know I love You.”

“Take care of My sheep,” said Jesus.

Then Jesus asked a third time, “Simon, son of John, do you love Me?”

Peter was hurt that Jesus asked him a third time. “Lord, You know everything,” he said. “You know that I love You.”

“Feed My sheep,” said Jesus.

Three times Peter had said he didn’t know Jesus, standing by a charcoal fire. Now, by another charcoal fire, Jesus gave him three chances to say he loved Him. Jesus was forgiving Peter, and giving him a new start. And He was giving him a job: to take care of His people, like a shepherd looks after sheep.

Then Jesus said to him, “Follow Me.”

The same words Jesus said on the very first day.

Read it in your Bible: John 21:1–19

Dear Jesus, thank you that you forgive us and give us a fresh start, like you did for Peter. Yes, Lord, you know that I love you. Help me to follow you. Amen.

study_questions.question: What did Jesus have ready for the disciples when they came to the shore?
study_questions.answer: A charcoal fire with fish cooking on it, and some bread. He had made them breakfast.

study_questions.question: How many times did Jesus ask Peter, “Do you love Me?” Why do you think He asked that many times?
study_questions.answer: Three times, one for each time Peter had said he didn’t know Jesus. Jesus was forgiving Peter and giving him a fresh start.

study_questions.question: After forgiving Peter, Jesus gave him a job: “Feed My sheep.” What does that tell us about how Jesus treats people who have failed?
study_questions.answer: That He doesn’t give up on them. He forgives them, and still has good work for them to do.

fields.title: Go and Tell the World
fields.body_html:
“And surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age.” — Matthew 28:20

After He rose from the dead, Jesus appeared to His followers many times over forty days. He showed them that He was really alive, in many different ways. Once He even appeared to more than five hundred people at the same time (1 Corinthians 15:6). And He talked with them about the kingdom of God.

One day the eleven disciples went to a mountain in Galilee, where Jesus had told them to go. When they saw Jesus, they worshipped Him. But some of them still weren’t sure.

Then Jesus came to them and said:

“All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me. So go and make disciples of all nations. Baptise them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. And teach them to obey everything I have commanded you. And surely I am with you always, to the very end of the age.”

Jesus was giving His followers the most important job in the world.

“All authority in heaven and on earth” means that Jesus is in charge of everything. He is King over everything.

“Make disciples of all nations” means: go everywhere, to every country, to every people, and help people to follow Jesus. Do you remember God’s very first promise to Abraham, that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him? Now it was going to come true. The good news about Jesus was for the whole world.

“Baptise them” means that people who believe in Jesus are baptised, as a sign that they belong to Him.

“Teach them to obey” means helping them to live the way Jesus taught: loving God and loving other people.

And then the most wonderful promise of all: “I am with you always.” Jesus wasn’t sending His friends out on their own. He would be with them every day, wherever they went, until the end of time.

Those eleven men were just ordinary people, mostly fishermen. They weren’t rich or powerful. And they were being asked to tell the whole world about Jesus!

But they did. And the people they told told other people, who told other people, all over the world, for two thousand years. And that is how the good news about Jesus has come to you.

That job hasn’t finished yet. Jesus still says to His followers, “Go and make disciples.” And He still says, “I am with you always.”

Read it in your Bible: Matthew 28:16–20

Dear Jesus, thank you that the good news about you is for the whole world. Thank you that you are with me always. Please help me to tell other people about you. Amen.

study_questions.question: What job did Jesus give His disciples?
study_questions.answer: To go and make disciples of all nations, baptising them and teaching them to obey everything He commanded.

study_questions.question: What promise did Jesus give them?
study_questions.answer: “I am with you always, to the very end of the age.”

study_questions.question: The good news about Jesus has been passed on for two thousand years, all the way to you. Who passed it on to you, and who could you pass it on to?
study_questions.answer: Talk about the people who told your family about Jesus, then think of someone you could tell or invite.

Jesus still says to His followers, “Go and make disciples.” And He still says, “I am with you always.” Read it in your Bible: Matthew 28:16–20 Dear Jesus, thank you that the good news about you is for the whole world. Thank you that you are with me always. Please help me to tell other people about you. Amen.

fields.title: Jesus Goes Up to Heaven
fields.body_html:
“This same Jesus, who has been taken from you into heaven, will come back in the same way you have seen Him go into heaven.” — Acts 1:11

Forty days after Jesus rose from the dead, He met with His disciples for the last time. He told them, “Don’t leave Jerusalem. Wait for the gift My Father promised. In a few days you will be baptised with the Holy Spirit.”

“Lord,” the disciples asked, “is now the time when You will make Israel a great kingdom again?”

“It’s not for you to know the times and dates the Father has set,” Jesus said. “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes on you. And you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.”

Then Jesus led them out of the city, as far as Bethany. He lifted up His hands and blessed them.

And while He was blessing them, He was taken up into heaven, right before their eyes. A cloud hid Him from their sight.

The disciples stood there, staring up into the sky, watching the place where He had gone.

Suddenly two men dressed in white were standing beside them. They were angels.

“Men of Galilee,” they said, “why are you standing here looking into the sky? This same Jesus, who has been taken from you into heaven, will come back in the same way you have seen Him go.”

Jesus had gone back to heaven, to His Father. But He hadn’t gone for ever. One day, He will come back.

And the disciples didn’t go home sad. They worshipped Jesus. And they went back to Jerusalem filled with great joy, and they spent their time in the temple, praising God.

Why were they so happy? Because they knew that Jesus was alive. They knew that He was now King in heaven, with all authority. They knew that He was with them always, just as He had promised. They knew that He would come back one day. And they knew that the Holy Spirit was coming soon, to give them power.

So they waited and prayed in Jerusalem. They didn’t know exactly what would happen next. But it was going to be amazing.

And that is where the Life of Jesus ends, and where the next part of the story begins: the story of how a small group of ordinary people took the good news about Jesus all the way to the ends of the earth.

Read it in your Bible: Acts 1:1–11; Luke 24:50–53

Dear Jesus, thank you that you are King in heaven, and that you will come back one day. Thank you for sending the Holy Spirit. Help me to be your witness wherever I go. Amen.

study_questions.question: What did Jesus tell the disciples to wait for in Jerusalem?
study_questions.answer: The gift the Father promised: the Holy Spirit, who would give them power to be His witnesses.

study_questions.question: What did the two angels say when the disciples were staring up into the sky?
study_questions.answer: That this same Jesus who had been taken into heaven would come back one day in the same way.

study_questions.question: Why were the disciples full of joy, even though Jesus had gone?
study_questions.answer: Because they knew He was alive and King in heaven, that He was always with them, that the Holy Spirit was coming, and that Jesus would come back one day.
